report:
**Conclusion: no—the evidence does not support that answer.** Offering HIV self-testing (HIVST) *in addition to* usual HIV-testing services generally causes more people to test, at least in the study settings and timeframes evaluated.

The strongest evidence is randomized-trial meta-analysis. A 2021 systematic review of 13 randomized controlled trials in general populations found that HIVST increased testing uptake versus standard services (risk ratio **2.09**, 95% CI 1.69–2.58; moderate-certainty evidence). In practical terms, people offered self-tests were about twice as likely to test during follow-up.  
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2589537021002716

A separate 2020 meta-analysis focused on key populations also found greater uptake with HIVST than standard testing (RR **1.45**, 95% CI 1.20–1.75).  
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-020-01835-z

For the narrower question of offering self-testing as an *additional option in health facilities*, WHO’s review concluded uptake may be comparable to or higher than standard facility testing, and WHO recommends facility-based HIVST as an additional testing option. This wording reflects some uncertainty and variation by setting—not evidence of no effect.  
https://www.who.int/news/item/22-07-2023-who-recommends-optimizing-hiv-testing-services

**Important qualification:** more testing does not automatically guarantee equivalent follow-up. One review reported lower linkage to care/antiretroviral treatment after HIVST than after standard services, underscoring the need for easy confirmatory testing and linkage support after a reactive self-test.  
https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0245498
